level_1.text: Cohesin (comprising subunits RAD21, SMC1, and SMC3) and the zinc finger transcription factor CTCF exhibit substantial overlap in binding sites across mammalian chromosomes, with each site containing a conserved CTCF consensus sequence. Chromatin immunoprecipitation reveals lineage- and stage-specific Rad21 recruitment to CTCF at all Ig loci, where these numerous CTCF/cohesin sites likely form the bases of multiloop rosette structures that compact during Ig heavy chain rearrangement. Additionally, evolutionarily conserved CTCF and cohesin (RAD21/SMC3) binding sites are identified within unmethylated regions ∼5 kb downstream of the PLAGL1 differentially methylated region and within the PLAGL1 3' untranslated region (UTR). These cohesin and CTCF binding sites also function as cis-regulatory elements (CREs) for runx1, as they recruit RNA polymerase II (RNAPII).

Cohesin and CTCF exhibit distinct genomic binding patterns and functional roles, with cohesin-non-CTCF (CNC) sites in primary mouse liver coinciding with master regulators, enhancer-markers, and liver-specific expressed genes, whereas co-localized sites often align with insulator functions. Low intestinal carbohydrate digestive enzyme activity was reported although there was no abnormality found in pancreatic function. questions.body: Which pathological conditions are caused by mutations in the CYLD gene?
ideal_answer: Since loss of CYLD expression can be observed in different types of human cancer, it is now well established that CYLD acts as a tumor suppressor gene. Pathogenic mutations in CYLD can be identified in patients affected with Brooke-Spiegler syndrome, (Familial) Cylindromatosis or multiple familial trichoepithelioma. CYLD expression has also been reported to be  dramatically downregulated in basal cell carcinoma (BCC), the most common cancer in humans.

level_1.text: Molecular genetic analyses of trichoepithelioma (TE) cases identified distinct *CYLD* gene alterations: a 35-year-old woman with multiple facial TEs harbored a novel heterozygous c.1843delT frameshift mutation, which was also present in a heterozygous state in her TE tumor cells and served as an adjunct to histopathological diagnosis; a separate molecular biologic study of peripheral blood revealed a novel splice site c.2041+1 G>T mutation; and a novel splicing mutation was identified in a Taiwanese family with multiple familial trichoepithelioma. In primary classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL), interphase cytogenetics detected a (sub)clonal biallelic *CYLD* deletion in 1 of 29 cases, while signal patterns indicating decreased *CYLD* copy numbers were observed in 10 of 29 primary cases.

The study aimed to comprehensively ascertain the extent and severity of clinical features in affected individuals from 2 large families with proven heterozygous mutations in the CYLD locus, correlating these findings with the 3 appendageal tumor predisposition syndromes associated with such germline mutations: familial cylindromatosis, Brooke-Spiegler syndrome, and multiple familial trichoepitheliomas.

Familial cylindromatosis, a benign skin tumor disorder, is caused by mutations in the *CYLD* tumor suppressor gene located on chromosome 16q21-13, distinct from the previously mapped candidate MTF locus at 9p21. Specific genetic variants identified include a frameshift mutation designated 2253delG, which demonstrates that a single mutation can result in distinct clinical and histologic expressions, and a recurrent R758X nonsense mutation (2272C>T) found in affected individuals across multiple ethnic families. The development of cylindromatosis is driven by mutation and loss of heterozygosity of the *CYLD* gene.

A case of Brooke-Spiegler syndrome is presented featuring a novel germline deep intronic mutation in the *CYLD* gene that induces intronic exonization, accompanied by diverse somatic mutations and unusual histology. This deep intronic mutation resulting in exonization, along with somatic sequence mutations causing exon skipping, represents hitherto unreported genetic mechanisms involving the *CYLD* gene in patients with Brooke-Spiegler syndrome.

Patients with heterozygous germline truncating mutations in the *CYLD* gene develop multiple primary hair follicle-related tumours, which may include both highly patterned cylindromas and highly disorganized spiradenomas within the same individual.

While early studies implicated the *PTCH* gene (chromosome 9q22.3) in the etiopathogenesis of MFT, recent investigations of patients exhibiting the MFT clinical phenotype have identified mutations in the *CYLD* gene (chromosome 16q12-q13), which is responsible for BSS.

Multiple trichoepitheliomas (TEs), particularly in familial contexts, are associated with germline heterozygous mutations in the *CYLD* gene, a finding that serves as an adjunct to histopathological diagnosis.

Mutations in the *CYLD* gene are identified as the genetic basis for Multicentric Familial Trichoepithelioma (MFT) across multiple cohorts, including three distinct Chinese families and a Taiwanese pedigree. A single family was described exhibiting both Familial Cylindroma (FC) and MFT phenotypes associated with a *CYLD* mutation. Specific novel mutations identified include a splicing mutation (IVS12 + 1 G-->A) in the Taiwanese pedigree, alongside other unspecified novel mutations in Chinese families.

Germline mutations in the tumour-suppressor gene *CYLD* predispose individuals to disfiguring cutaneous appendageal tumours, with the highly organised cylindroma serving as the defining lesion. *CYLD* is established as a tumor suppressor due to its dramatic downregulation in basal cell carcinoma (BCC), the most common human cancer, and its loss across various other human malignancies. Functional studies demonstrate that expressing a catalytically inactive form of *CYLD* (CYLD(C/S)) in tumorigenic epidermal cells, which mimics identified human tumor mutations and competes with endogenous *CYLD*, results in enhanced cell proliferation and inhibited apoptosis. Contrasting with previous findings of benign tumour development, evidence indicates that *CYLD* mutations in tumorigenic epidermal cells (carrying prior mutations) increase carcinoma aggressiveness and epidermal cancer malignancy, primarily by enhancing the expression of angiogenic factors. Additionally, new *CYLD* mutations identified in skin appendage tumors confirm that aspartic acid 681 is essential for the protein’s deubiquitinase activity.

Maspin downregulation is characterized in cylindromas, trichoepitheliomas, and spiradenomas harboring functional inactivating mutations of CYLD, providing in vivo evidence in human tumors of a correlation between impaired CYLD function and decreased Maspin expression.

Brooke-Spiegler syndrome, familial cylindromatosis, and familial trichoepithelioma are rare, autosomal-dominant genetic predispositions for benign tumors of skin appendages, characterized by multiple skin appendage tumors caused by various mutations in the CYLD gene localized on chromosome 16q12-q13.

Germline mutations in the *CYLD* tumor suppressor gene, located on chromosome 16q, underlie the phenotypes of Brooke-Spiegler syndrome (BSS), familial cylindromatosis, and multiple familial trichoepithelioma. These conditions are characterized by various *CYLD* mutations, including novel germline variants identified in specific cases, such as a Slovak patient with BSS, which expand the catalogue of known mutations. In BSS, both germline *CYLD* mutations and various somatic mutations within lesional tissues have been identified.
The disease gene for BSS was mapped to chromosomal region 16q12-13, and mutations in the CYLD gene were identified in affected families.

level_1.text: Imetelstat (GRN163L), a potent telomerase inhibitor and specific antagonist of the reverse transcriptase activity of telomerase, effectively targets cancer stem cells (CSCs) and tumor-initiating cells (TICs) across multiple malignancies by inhibiting telomerase activity and inducing telomere shortening. In breast and pancreatic cancer cell lines, imetelstat inhibited telomerase activity in both bulk tumor cells and CSC subpopulations, depleting CSCs. In glioblastoma (GBM), treatment produced dose-dependent telomerase inhibition with an IC50 of 0.45 micromol/L; long-term exposure led to progressive telomere shortening, reduced proliferation, decreased tumor growth, and eventual cell death in GBM tumor-initiating cells. In multiple myeloma (MM), two weeks of imetelstat exposure to CSCs isolated from cell lines and primary clinical specimens resulted in significant telomere length reduction and inhibition of clonogenic growth both in vitro and in vivo. Imetelstat (GRN163L), a telomerase inhibitor, exerts off-target effects on the cytoskeleton. Following the reversal of long-term Imetelstat treatment, telomerase extension is less processive during the first few weeks, a period characterized by the failure of Cajal bodies to deliver telomerase RNA to telomeres.

Imetelstat (GRN163L), a potent and specific telomerase inhibitor and the only drug of its class currently in clinical trials, inhibits telomerase activity in cancer cell lines and counters telomerase activation. Beyond telomerase inhibition, GRN163L induces morphological cell rounding changes that are independent of hTR expression or telomere length. As a small oligonucleotide targeted therapy, Imetelstat is discussed alongside other telomerase-based approaches, including telomerase as an immunotherapy and gene therapy utilizing telomerase promoter-driven oncolytic viruses.

Imetelstat sodium (GRN163L) is a 13-mer oligonucleotide N3'→P5' thio-phosphoramidate lipid conjugated to a 5'-palmitoyl group, representing the latest generation of potent human telomerase inhibitors that target the template region of the human functional telomerase RNA (hTR) subunit. Preclinical trials demonstrate that this compound inhibits telomerase activity in multiple cancer cell lines and in vivo xenograft mouse models.

Imetelstat, a thio-phosphoramidate oligonucleotide inhibitor of telomerase, demonstrated dose-dependent inhibition of telomerase activity in esophageal cancer cells. Long-term treatment with imetelstat decreased cell growth in these cells, exhibiting different kinetics regarding telomere lengths.

level_2.text: Imetelstat (GRN163L), a 13-mer oligonucleotide N3'→P5' thio-phosphoramidate lipid conjugated to a 5'-palmitoyl group, is a potent, specific telomerase inhibitor and the only drug of its class currently in clinical trials. It targets the template region of the human functional telomerase RNA (hTR) subunit to inhibit the reverse transcriptase activity of telomerase. Preclinical data demonstrate dose-dependent telomerase inhibition across multiple malignancies, including an IC50 of 0.45 micromol/L in glioblastoma (GBM). In GBM, long-term exposure induces progressive telomere shortening, reduced proliferation, decreased tumor growth, and eventual cell death in tumor-initiating cells (TICs). In breast and pancreatic cancer cell lines, imetelstat depletes cancer stem cells (CSCs) by inhibiting telomerase activity in both bulk tumor cells and CSC subpopulations. level_1.text: In *Bacillus anthracis*, the toxin genes *cya*, *lef*, and *pag* constitute a regulon whose transcription is activated in trans by the regulatory gene *atxA*. In *atxA*+ strains, this expression is enhanced by two physiologically significant signals: elevated CO2/bicarbonate and temperature.

In *Bacillus anthracis*, the regulation of the anthrax toxin activator gene (*atxA*) is primarily driven by temperature, which directly affects AtxA synthesis, rather than by CO2/bicarbonate levels. Although *atxA* is associated with CO2-enhanced non-toxin gene expression, temperature is the specific environmental factor governing AtxA production.

Two major apparent transcriptional start sites, designated P1 and P2, were identified at positions 731 bp and 625 bp, respectively, upstream of the translation-initiation codon of *capB*. Transcription initiated from both P1 and P2 is activated by *atxA* and *acpA*, a process that appears to be stimulated by bicarbonate. Deletion analysis of the upstream region of the *cap* promoter demonstrated that activation by both *atxA* and *acpA* requires a DNA segment of 70 bp extending upstream of the P1 site.

AtxA is part of the sap and eag regulatory network in both in vitro (in the presence of CO2) and in vivo contexts. Transcription initiated from promoters P1 and P2 is activated by both atxA and acpA, with this activation appearing to be stimulated by bicarbonate. Notably, transcription of atxA itself does not appear to differ between cells grown in 5% CO2 and those grown in air.

Bioinformatic analyses of the 475 amino acid sequence of AtxA identified DNA binding motifs and regions homologous to proteins associated with the phosphoenolpyruvate: carbohydrate phosphotransferase system (PTS), specifically revealing two PTS regulation domains (PRD) that are generally regulated by phosphorylation/dephosphorylation at conserved histidine residues.

Screening of transposon-insertion libraries identified 17 mutants expressing CO2-enhanced atxA-dependent beta-galactosidase activity; DNA sequence analysis of their insertion sites revealed that 10 mutants harbored independent insertions on the 185-kb toxin plasmid pXO1 that did not map to the toxin genes.

Upon infection of a mammalian host, *Bacillus anthracis* responds to host cues, specifically elevated temperature (37°C) and bicarbonate/CO2 concentrations, by increasing the expression of virulence factors, including anthrax toxins and the extracellular capsular layer. The transcription of major *Bacillus anthracis* virulence genes is triggered by CO2, a signal that mimics the host environment.

In *Bacillus anthracis*, elevated CO2 levels enhance the transcription of toxin genes, an effect strictly dependent on the pXO1 gene *atxA*, which encodes a transactivator of anthrax toxin synthesis; this CO2-enhanced transcription is absent in *atx4*-null mutants. While *atxA* expression itself is not influenced by CO2/bicarbonate levels, the steady-state level of *atxA* mRNA is five- to sixfold higher in cells grown at 37°C compared to 28°C under elevated CO2/bicarbonate conditions. Transcriptome analysis reveals that *atxA* regulates genes beyond the structural anthrax toxin proteins, including non-toxin proteins whose synthesis is influenced by elevated CO2 and *atxA*. Furthermore, these findings link virulence factor production to carbohydrate metabolism and provide the first mechanistic explanation for *AtxA* transcriptional activity.

Cultures grown with elevated CO(2)/bicarbonate exhibited increased AtxA dimer/monomer ratios and increased AtxA activity relative to cultures without added CO(2)/bicarbonate, indicating that this host-associated signal enhances AtxA function by shifting the dimer/monomer equilibrium towards the dimeric state.

level_2.text: In *Bacillus anthracis*, the *atxA* gene on the 185-kb plasmid pXO1 encodes a 475-amino acid transactivator that regulates the *cya*, *lef*, and *pag* toxin regulon and non-toxin genes, including *capB*. While *atxA* transcription is primarily driven by temperature—with steady-state mRNA levels 5- to 6-fold higher at 37°C than at 28°C under elevated CO2/bicarbonate conditions—its activity is modulated by host-associated signals. Elevated CO2/bicarbonate does not alter *atxA* transcription but enhances AtxA function by shifting the dimer/monomer equilibrium toward the dimeric state, thereby increasing activity. questions.body: Which syndromes are associated with mutations in the EZH2 gene?
ideal_answer: EZH2 mutations that cause Weaver syndrome are primarily missense variants and the rare truncating mutations reported to date are in the last exon, suggesting that simple haploinsufficiency is unlikely to be generating the overgrowth phenotype although the exact mechanism has not yet been determined. Recent studies have shown that EZH2 mutations are often associated with RUNX1 mutations in MDS patients, although its pathological function remains to be addressed. These data show that mutations in EZH2 cause Weaver syndrome. The EZH2 gene is a homolog of the Drosophila Polycomb group (PcG) gene enhancer of zest, a crucial regulator of homeotic gene expression.

Loss-of-function mutations of EZH2, a catalytic component of polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), are observed in ~\n10% of patients with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), but are rare in acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). Constitutional NSD1 and EZH2 mutations cause Sotos and Weaver syndromes respectively, overgrowth syndromes with considerable phenotypic overlap. Mutations at tyrosine 641 (Y641F, Y641N, Y641S and Y641H) in the SET domain of EZH2 have been identified in patients with certain subtypes of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). The EZH2 gene is involved in the pathogenesis of 7q35-q36 aberrations in myeloid leukaemia.

Constitutional mutations in *NSD1* and *EZH2* cause Sotos syndrome and Weaver syndrome, respectively, which are overgrowth syndromes characterized by considerable phenotypic overlap. *NSD1* mutations associated with Sotos syndrome are loss-of-function variants, primarily consisting of truncating mutations or missense mutations at key residues within functional domains.

Mutations in *EZH2* cause Weaver syndrome, with the mutation spectrum showing considerable overlap with inactivating somatic *EZH2* mutations reported in myeloid malignancies. The pathogenic variants are primarily missense, while the rare truncating mutations identified to date are located in the last exon; this distribution suggests that simple haploinsufficiency is unlikely to generate the overgrowth phenotype, although the exact mechanism remains undetermined.

Weaver syndrome and Sotos syndrome exhibit considerable phenotypic overlap; consequently, the identification of an *EZH2* mutation serves as an objective means to confirm subtle presentations of Weaver syndrome and to distinguish it from Sotos syndrome.

Somatic mutations in Polycomb group (PcG) genes, specifically inactivating mutations in *EZH2* and *ASXL1*, are frequently identified in myelodysplastic disorders, including myelodysplastic syndromes (MDSs) and MDS/myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN) overlap disorders. Among premenopausal women, current use of oral contraceptives (OCs) was consistently associated with an increased risk of meningiomas (OR 1.8, 95% CI 1.1–2.9). In contrast, findings for postmenopausal women using hormone replacement therapy (HRT) are mixed: one analysis reported no significant elevation in risk for current HRT users (OR 1.1, 95% CI 0.74–1.67), while another identified a higher risk among current HRT users compared to never users (HR 1.79, 95% CI 1.18–2.71). A retrospective study of over 350,000 women (including ~1,400 meningioma cases) suggested the risk was approximately twice as high in postmenopausal HRT users versus non-users. Specifically, estradiol-only therapy was accompanied by a slightly increased risk of meningioma. However, the relationship between current use of exogenous hormones and meningioma remains unclear and not definitive, limited by small numbers of patients currently on oral hormone medications and a lack of hormone receptor data for meningioma tumors. level_1.text: 3-iodothyronamine (T(1)AM), a novel endogenous thyroid hormone relative that interacts with trace amine-associated receptors (plasma membrane G protein-coupled receptors), exerts negative inotropic and chronotropic effects; specifically, acute exposure to 20 microM T(1)AM in adult rat cardiomyocytes decreased the amplitude and duration of the calcium transient. In contrast, triiodothyronine (T3) in normal porcine myocardium did not alter the extent of isometric force generation but accelerated the time course of force development (p < 0.05) and increased the calcium transient (p < 0.001). Following epinephrine-induced myocardial depression, T3 accelerated intracellular calcium transients and reduced diastolic calcium. Evidence of increased force amplitudes at unaltered intracellular calcium transient amplitudes and reduced calcium time integral indicates T3 sensitizes the contractile apparatus for calcium. These findings demonstrate that thyroid state influences the time course of the calcium transient, consistent with the abbreviated duration of contraction observed in the hyperthyroid state.

questions.body: What is the role of extracellular signal-related kinases 1 and 2 (ERK1/2) proteins in craniosynostosis?

This hypersensitivity to DNA cross-linking agents and the high frequencies of induced chromosomal aberrations serve as diagnostic properties for the disease. Additionally, semiconservative DNA synthesis is severely inhibited in FA cells. These features—chromosomal aberrations, hypersensitivity to DNA crosslinking agents, and predisposition to malignancy—suggest a fundamental anomaly of DNA repair in Fanconi anemia.

Fanconi's anemia cells, characterized by chromosomal sensitivity to crosslinking agents and a defect in the "unhooking" of linked polynucleotide strands, also exhibit chromosomal sensitivity to ethyl methanesulfonate and ionizing radiation, implying overlapping repair systems.

Fanconi anemia (FA) is an autosomal disorder characterized by genome instability, manifested by defects in DNA repair, hypersensitivity to DNA crosslinking agents, and a high degree of chromosomal aberrations. Clinical phenotypes include developmental abnormalities, early-onset bone marrow failure, and a predisposition to cancer.

level_2.text: Fanconi anemia (FA) is an autosomal disorder characterized by genome instability, developmental abnormalities, early-onset bone marrow failure, and a predisposition to cancer. At the cellular level, FA is defined by a fundamental anomaly in DNA repair, specifically a defect in the "unhooking" of linked polynucleotide strands, which results in a high frequency of spontaneous chromosomal aberrations and chromosome breakage. This instability is markedly exacerbated by exposure to DNA crosslinking agents, including DNA interstrand crosslink agents, to which FA cells exhibit unusual hypersensitivity, leading to an abnormal increase in chromosomal damage. Additionally, FA cells display chromosomal sensitivity to ethyl methanesulfonate and ionizing radiation, implying overlapping repair systems, and suffer from severely inhibited semiconservative DNA synthesis. The combination of chromosomal aberrations, hypersensitivity to DNA crosslinking agents, and malignancy predisposition serves as diagnostic properties for the disease.

level_1.text: Research has investigated the structural and functional effects of familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)-linked point mutations in cardiac troponin C (cTnC), specifically A8V, C84Y, E134D, and D145E. These studies utilized PRE data to assess the impact of the A8V mutation on the dynamic equilibrium between closed and open conformations of the regulatory N-domain of isolated cTnC. Additionally, the effects of A8V, E134D, and D145E mutations on the properties of the C-domain sites were examined. The functional consequences of these mutations were evaluated by measuring the Ca(2+) sensitivity of force development in reconstituted thin filaments, including assessments of the response to calcium upon phosphorylation of cardiac troponin I (cTnI) by protein kinase A.

Clinical and functional characterization of a novel *TNNC1* A31S mutation in a pediatric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) proband with multiple episodes of ventricular fibrillation and aborted sudden cardiac death indicates the mutation is associated with HCM pathogenesis and may predispose to a fatal arrhythmogenic subtype. In contrast, the *TNNC1* A23Q mutant exhibits HCM-like properties characterized by increased Ca(2+) sensitivity of force and normal levels of ATPase inhibition. Comprehensive open reading frame/splice site mutation analysis of *TNNC1* in 1025 unrelated HCM patients enrolled over 10 years identified additional novel missense mutations: A8V, C84Y, E134D, and D145E.

Mutations in *TNNC1*-encoded cardiac troponin C (cTnC) predispose to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) and ventricular fibrillation, including the TNNC1-A31S variant. A novel, rare frameshift mutation, c.363dupG (p.Gln122AlafsX30), was identified in a 19-year-old male with HCM and sudden cardiac death, demonstrating familial segregation. Additionally, the cTnC L29Q mutation, found in familial HCM, hinders the transduction of protein kinase A-dependent phosphorylation signals from cardiac troponin I to C.

The L29Q mutation, which involves a leucine-to-glutamine exchange at position 29 in the nonfunctional calcium-binding site of cardiac troponin C (cTnC), enhances the Ca(2+)-binding characteristics of cTnC and, when incorporated into cardiac myocytes, alters myocyte contractility.

questions.body: What is known about clinical efficacy of ceftriaxone for treatment of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis?
ideal_answer: There have been a few case reports to suggest that ceftriaxone can be effective for treatment of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. However, other case reports did not report clinical benefit of ceftriaxone therapy for ALS. Ceftriaxone has been reported to reduce neuronal damage in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis a through increased expression and activity of the glutamate transporter, GLT1. Clinical trials investigating potential clinical benefits of ceftriaxone in ALS are ongoing.

level_1.text: Ceftriaxone, a beta-lactam antibiotic, exerts neuroprotective effects by upregulating the expression and activity of the astrocyte-specific glutamate excitatory amino acid transporter 2 (EAAT2/GLT-1). This mechanism mitigates glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity, a pathological process implicated in acute and chronic neurological disorders including stroke/ischemia, temporal lobe epilepsy, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), Alzheimer disease, human immunodeficiency virus 1-associated dementia, and malignant glioma growth. In genetic animal models of ALS, specifically mutant superoxide dismutase 1 transgenic mice, ceftriaxone treatment delayed neuronal loss and decline in muscle strength, thereby prolonging survival. Additionally, ceftriaxone demonstrated neuroprotection in in-vitro models of neuronal ischemia and motor neuron degeneration by inhibiting neuronal cell death associated with glutamate toxicity.

Rothstein et al. reported that beta-lactam antibiotics, specifically penicillin and the cephalosporin ceftriaxone, are potential therapeutic agents for neurological disorders such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), acting by modulating the expression of the glutamate transporter GLT1 via gene activation.

Although promising Stage 2 data were reported, the Stage 3 trial of ceftriaxone in ALS did not demonstrate clinical efficacy. Specific case reports describe mixed outcomes: one verifiable case of progressive motor neuron disease consistent with ALS resolved during treatment with intravenous ceftriaxone combined with oral atovaquone and mefloquine (anti-Babesia therapy), whereas two other patients with lateral amyotrophic sclerosis showed no positive results after receiving empirical intravenous ceftriaxone at a dose of 2 g/24 hours for three weeks.

level_1.text: Ichthyosis follicularis, alopecia, and photophobia (IFAP) syndrome is characterized by the triad of ichthyosis follicularis, alopecia, and photophobia, with clinical findings overlapping with dermotrichic syndrome. Reported variants include IFAP-PPK syndrome, which presents with coexisting psoriasiform lesions and palmoplantar keratoderma. Ocular findings are a distinct feature of the syndrome, and acitretin has been utilized as a treatment modality.

The ichthyosis follicular with atrichia and photophobia syndrome (IFAP) is a rare X-linked multiple congenital malformation syndrome characterized by the triad of follicular ichthyosis, atrichia, and photophobia. In women heterozygous for IFAP, linear lesions reflect lyonization.

Mutations in *MBTPS2* cause a broad spectrum of X-linked genodermatoses, including IFAP (ichthyosis follicularis; atrichia and photophobia) syndrome (OMIM 308205) with or without BRESHECK (brain anomalies, retardation of mentality and growth, ectodermal dysplasia, skeletal malformations, Hirschsprung disease, ear deformity and deafness, eye hypoplasia, cleft palate, cryptorchidism, and kidney dysplasia/hypoplasia) syndrome, keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans (KFSD; OMIM 308800), and an X-linked form of Olmsted syndrome. A recurrent intronic mutation in *MBTPS2* (c.671-9T>G) was identified in a Chinese patient presenting with the typical IFAP triad (ichthyosis, atrichia, and photophobia), accompanied by pachyonychia, palmoplantar and periorificial keratoderma, and features reminiscent of Olmsted syndrome.

The clinical phenotype encompasses the shared features of dermotrichic syndrome and ichthyosis follicularis-alopecia-photophobia (IFAP) syndrome, specifically including IFAP-characteristic photophobia and recurrent respiratory infections, as well as dermotrichic-specific nail anomalies, hypohydrosis, megacolon, and vertebral defects, alongside additional findings of enamel dysplasia, renal anomalies, and inguinal hernia.

Ichthyosis follicularis, atrichia, and photophobia (IFAP) syndrome is a rare congenital neuroichthyosis characterized by the triad of ichthyosis follicularis, atrichia, and photophobia. The clinical phenotype exhibits significant variability and severity, ranging from typical presentations to severe manifestations including ichthyosis follicular, brain anomalies, global developmental delay, Hirschsprung disease, kidney hypoplasia, follicular hyperkeratosis, chronic candidiasis, keratitis, seizures, mental retardation, and inguinal hernia. Documented cases include an 18-month-old male infant and two unrelated female patients, with one specific patient presenting a severe IFAP/BRESHECK phenotype encompassing the aforementioned multisystemic complications.

questions.body: Is there any algorithm for enhancer identification from chromatin state?
ideal_answer: yes

Yes. RFECS is a random-forest based algorithm for enhancer identification from chromatin state. It integrates histone modification profiles for the identification of enhancers, and can be used to identify enhancers in a number of cell-types. RFECS not only leads to more accurate and precise prediction of enhancers than previous methods, but also helps identify the most informative and robust set of three chromatin marks for enhancer prediction.

However, only a limited number of cell types or chromatin marks have previously been investigated for this purpose, leaving the question unanswered whether there exists an optimal set of histone modifications for enhancer prediction in different cell types. Here, we address this issue by exploring genome-wide profiles of 24 histone modifications in two distinct human cell types, embryonic stem cells and lung fibroblasts. We developed a Random-Forest based algorithm, RFECS (Random Forest based Enhancer identification from Chromatin States) to integrate histone modification profiles for identification of enhancers, and used it to identify enhancers in a number of cell-types. We show that RFECS not only leads to more accurate and precise prediction of enhancers than previous methods, but also helps identify the most informative and robust set of three chromatin marks for enhancer prediction.

level_1.text: 3,5-diiodothyropropionic acid (DITPA), a unique analog that binds to both α- and β-type thyroid receptors (TRs) with relatively low affinity, exhibits a complex and contradictory profile in cardiac pathology. While DITPA treatment attenuates the acute inflammatory response and reduces myocardial infarct size, and has been noted to improve left ventricular function in heart failure as well as lower cholesterol, it simultaneously impairs baseline cardiac parameters in mice and can be fatal during in vivo acute myocardial ischemia/reperfusion (I/R). Furthermore, although DITPA improved specific hemodynamic and metabolic parameters, there was no evidence for symptomatic benefit in congestive heart failure.

The thyroid analog DITPA promotes healthy vasculature and beneficial chamber remodeling—likely via improved cell shape and vascular supply—independently of thyroid-related metabolic effects, a mechanism shared with T4. level_2.text: The Yamanaka factors, collectively designated as OSKM or 4TF, comprise the specific set of transcription factors Oct4 (also referred to as Oct3/4 or Pou5f1), Sox2, Klf4, and c-Myc (also referred to as Myc or cMYC). These factors, which are highly expressed in embryonic stem (ES) cells, regulate the developmental signaling network necessary for ES cell pluripotency. Their ectopic or over-expression serves as the basal condition for inducing pluripotency in both mouse and human somatic cells to generate induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells, and they are utilized with or without c-MYC. This gene set is distinct from the Thomson factors, which consist of Sox2, Oct3, Lin28, and Nanog.

level_1.text: Experiments restricting prohibitin function to mitochondria identify the processing of the dynamin-like GTPase OPA1, an essential component of the mitochondrial fusion machinery, as the central cellular process controlled by prohibitins. These results define, for the first time, a function of the middle domain of the Opa1 protein and demonstrate that mitochondrial retention of Opa1 protein is essential for normal embryogenesis.

In HeLa cells, two OPA1 protein isoforms were identified and characterized for their submitochondrial localization and complex formations, with evidence indicating the release of high molecular weight (high MW) Opa-1 isoforms from the mitochondria to the cytosol.

OPA1 (also known as Mgm1 in yeast) is a nuclear-encoded mitochondrial dynamin-related GTPase that facilitates mitochondrial fusion. Unlike other dynamin family members, OPA1 possesses an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence for import into mitochondria. Biochemical examinations and submitochondrial fractionation via sucrose density-gradient centrifugation reveal that OPA1 exists as two isoforms within the intermembrane space: the 88-kDa protein predominantly associates with the mitochondrial outer membrane, whereas the 93-kDa protein associates with the inner membrane. The human OPA1 protein is anchored to the mitochondrial inner membrane facing the intermembrane space, a localization regulated by proteolytic cleavage. Additionally, LRRK2 partially co-localizes with OPA1 at mitochondrial membranes, as well as with mitofusins or endosomal dynamin-1.

PKA phosphorylates perilipin, a lipid droplet surface protein that regulates lipase access to stored triglycerides for conversion into free fatty acids and glycerol in a phosphorylation-dependent manner. Optic atrophy 1 (OPA1), a protein known to regulate mitochondrial dynamics, functions as a dual-specificity A-kinase anchoring protein associated with lipid droplets.
Mitochondrial fusion is mediated by specific genes, including Mfn1 (mitofusin 1), Mfn2 (mitofusin 2), and Opa1 (optic atrophy 1).
Mitochondrial remodeling induced by fission inhibition via 15d-PGJ2 is characterized by molecular alterations in the mitochondrial fusion protein OPA1.

Mitofusin 2 and OPA1 regulate mitochondrial metabolism, where loss-of-function reduces oxygen consumption and substrate oxidation capacity. Mitochondrial fission and fusion mediators, specifically hFis1 and OPA1, modulate cellular senescence. Furthermore, the lack of mitochondrial retention of Opa1 is sufficient to cause a cellular Opa1 loss-of-function phenotype characterized by mitochondrial fragmentation and an inability to fuse.
Silencing of the mitochondrial protein OPA1 enhances mitochondrial Ca(2+) signaling and aldosterone production in H295R adrenocortical cells.
In COS-7 cells, the subcellular distribution of overexpressed mOPA1 largely overlapped with that of endogenous cytochrome c, a well-known mitochondrial marker.

Biochemical techniques, including mitochondrial isolation, digitonin extraction, protease protection assays, and carbonate extraction, established that mammalian Opa1 resides in the intermembrane space and is tightly bound to the inner membrane.

15d-PGJ2-induced mitochondrial fusion initially requires the presence of outer membrane proteins Mfn1 and Mfn2 and the inner membrane protein OPA1; subsequent mitochondrial changes involve increased degradation and ubiquitination of newly synthesized OPA1, alongside decreased expression of Mfn1 and Mfn2, which likely contribute to the loss of tubular rigidity, disorganization of cristae, and the formation of large, swollen, degenerated, and dysfunctional mitochondria.

level_2.text: OPA1 (optic atrophy 1; yeast Mgm1) is a nuclear-encoded mitochondrial dynamin-related GTPase essential for mitochondrial fusion, functioning alongside Mfn1 and Mfn2. OPA1 exists as two isoforms: an 88-kDa protein predominantly associated with the outer membrane and a 93-kDa protein associated with the inner membrane, with localization regulated by proteolytic cleavage. In HeLa cells, high molecular weight OPA1 isoforms are released from mitochondria to the cytosol, while in COS-7 cells, overexpressed mOPA1 distribution overlaps with cytochrome c. Prohibitins control the processing of OPA1, defining a function for the middle domain of the OPA1 protein; mitochondrial retention of OPA1 is essential for normal embryogenesis, and its lack causes a loss-of-function phenotype characterized by mitochondrial fragmentation and an inability to fuse. snippets.text: Identifying associations between genotypes and gene expression levels using microarrays has enabled systematic interrogation of regulatory variation underlying complex phenotypes. This approach has vast potential for functional characterization of disease states, but its prohibitive cost, given hundreds to thousands of individual samples from populations have to be genotyped and expression profiled, has limited its widespread application.RESULTS: Here we demonstrate that genomic regions with allele-specific expression (ASE) detected by sequencing cDNA are highly enriched for cis-acting expression quantitative trait loci (cis-eQTL) identified by profiling of 500 animals in parallel, with up to 90% agreement on the allele that is preferentially expressed. We also observed widespread noncoding and antisense ASE and identified several allele-specific alternative splicing variants.CONCLUSION: Monitoring ASE by sequencing cDNA from as little as one sample is a practical alternative to expression genetics for mapping cis-acting variation that regulates RNA transcription and processing.

snippets.text: To elucidate mechanisms involved in multiple sclerosis (MS), we studied genetic regulation of experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) in rats, assuming a conservation of pathogenic pathways. In this study, we focused on Eae23, originally identified to regulate EAE in a (LEW.1AV1xPVG.1AV1)F2 cross. Our aim was to determine whether one or more genes within the 67 Mb region regulate EAE and to define candidate risk genes.METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: We used high resolution quantitative trait loci (QTL) analysis in the 10th generation (G10) of an advanced intercross line (AIL) to resolve Eae23 into two QTLs that independently regulate EAE, namely Eae23a and Eae23b.

level_1.text: Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is a central eukaryotic trafficking process wherein clathrin-coated vesicles (CCVs) form at the plasma membrane to act as endocytic vectors, while also assembling at the trans-Golgi network (TGN) with unclear functional roles. The interaction between the clathrin N-terminal domain (TD) and endocytic accessory proteins has been targeted by the first reported small molecule inhibitors. Beyond canonical trafficking, clathrin forms elaborate tubulobulbar complexes with actin at intercellular attachment sites in the mammalian testis seminiferous epithelium. Additionally, exposure to 20- and 50-nm gold nanoparticles in mice increased clathrin immunoreactivity in placental tissues, with immunopositivity specifically observed in syncytiotrophoblasts and fetal endothelial cells.

Gene knockout studies have shed light on the very different physiological functions of IKKalpha and IKKbeta. After phosphorylation, the IKK phosphoacceptor sites on IkappaB serve as an essential part of a specific recognition site for E3RS(IkappaB/beta-TrCP), an SCF-type E3 ubiquitin ligase, thereby explaining how IKK controls IkappaB ubiquitination and degradation.

The multisubunit IKK complex, comprising catalytic subunits IKKα and IKKβ, serves as the convergence point for NF-κB-activating stimuli; both subunits phosphorylate IκB, creating a phosphoacceptor site that forms a specific degron recognized by the F-box component β-TrCP. This recognition couples IκB phosphorylation to ubiquitination via the SCF(β-TrCP) complex (also referred to as E3RS(IkappaB/beta-TrCP)), a highly efficient process that often results in complete IκBα degradation within minutes of stimulation. In vivo ablation of β-TrCP leads to accumulation of all IκBs and complete NF-κB inhibition. Sequence analysis reveals motif identity between CLU and β-TrCP. Valproic acid (VPA), an antiepileptic agent with histone deacetylase inhibitor (HDACi) activity, has been shown in preclinical models to sensitize glioblastoma (GBM) cells to radiation. Treatment of glioblastoma-derived stem cells (GDSCs) with HDAC inhibitors, including VPA and trichostatin A (TSA), significantly reduces cell proliferation rates and the expression of stem cell markers, indicating cellular differentiation. This differentiation into GBM phenotypes renders GDSCs susceptible to conventional cancer treatments, suggesting that HDAC inhibitor therapy may enhance the efficacy of standard therapeutic regimens for eliminating GDSCs.

In a retrospective review of 544 adults with glioblastoma (GB), 217 (40%) experienced seizures before the end of radiation therapy (RT), and 403 (74%) were taking an antiepileptic drug (AED) during RT, with 29 (7%) specifically taking valproic acid (VA). When the analysis was restricted to patients receiving concurrent temozolomide (TMZ), VA use was marginally associated with overall survival (OS) (P=.057; HR, 0.54; 95% CI, -0.09 to 1.17), independent of Radiation Therapy Oncology Group recursive partitioning analysis (RTOG RPA) class and seizure history.

Addition of valproic acid (VPA) to concurrent radiotherapy (RT) and temozolomide (TMZ) in patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma (GBM) is well tolerated and associated with prolonged survival. Specifically, patients using VPA in combination with TMZ demonstrated a median survival of 69 weeks (95% CI: 61.7–67.3) compared to 61 weeks (95% CI: 52.5–69.5) in the group without VPA, representing a 2-month survival advantage. This benefit was observed with a hazard ratio of 0.63 (95% CI: 0.43–0.92; P = .016) after adjusting for age, extent of resection, and O(6)-DNA methylguanine-methyltransferase promoter methylation status. These findings suggest that VPA administration may improve outcomes compared to historical data and merits further study.

level_1.text: Tarlov cysts, also known as spinal perineurial or perineural cysts, are uncommon nerve root lesions most frequently located in the sacral region, with rare occurrences in the cervical spine. While typically benign and asymptomatic, warranting simple monitoring, symptomatic cases exist, including rare instances of symptomatic cervical cysts and large sacral cysts initially misdiagnosed as adnexal masses and biopsied via laparoscopy. Management of symptomatic Tarlov cysts remains debated regarding the necessity of surgical intervention, whereas asymptomatic cases are generally followed. Additionally, spinal MRI scans have identified associations between sacral fractures draining into perineurial cysts.

level_2.text: Tarlov cysts (spinal perineurial/perineural cysts) are rare, often asymptomatic nerve-root lesions situated between the perineurium and endoneurium, typically near the dorsal root ganglion in the sacral spine, with rare cervical occurrences. While generally benign and managed via monitoring, symptomatic cases—such as large sacral cysts initially misdiagnosed as adnexal masses and biopsied via laparoscopy, or symptomatic cervical cysts—present debated management regarding surgical intervention. Imaging (ultrasound, CT, MRI, and CT myelography) has identified specific presentations, including a giant (6.7 × 6.4 × 6.6 cm) cyst originating from the right S-2 nerve root sleeve/sacral foramen with intrapelvic extension, multiloculated disseminated perineural cysts, and vertebral erosion causing photopenic areas. Additionally, spinal MRI scans have identified associations between sacral fractures draining into perineurial cysts.

level_1.text: Germline mutations in the aryl hydrocarbon receptor-interacting protein gene (*AIP*) are identified in approximately 25% of familial isolated pituitary adenoma (FIPA) kindreds. These mutations predispose individuals to young-onset pituitary tumours, most frequently GH- or prolactin-secreting adenomas, with the majority of affected patients belonging to FIPA families. A specific novel C-terminal nonsense mutation, Q315X, has been identified in a Japanese FIPA family.

Germline inactivating mutations in the aryl hydrocarbon receptor interacting protein (AIP) gene, located at genetic locus 11q13, are a major determinant in the pathogenesis of familial isolated pituitary adenoma (FIPA), identified in approximately 20% of FIPA families. These mutations are also present in about 3–5% of sporadic pituitary adenomas, with a specific predisposition for early-onset somatotropinomas and prolactinomas. The pathophysiology involves loss of heterozygosity at the 11q13 locus within the tumor. While AIP mutations primarily drive FIPA, rare extra-pituitary tumors have been described in AIP mutation-positive cases, and the identification of these mutations has expanded the understanding of inherited pituitary adenoma disorders.

Two Spanish Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenoma (FIPA) families were reported, one harboring a previously unreported *AIP* gene mutation in a familiar context and the other carrying an *AIP* R16H change, which supports the hypothesis that the R16H variant represents a variant of unknown significance.

Familial isolated pituitary adenomas (FIPA) remain of unknown etiology in a high percentage of cases, though the *AIP* gene plays a significant role in pathogenesis. Genetic analyses have identified specific *AIP* mutations, including the R81X variant, which selectively drives pituitary tumor development in patients presenting with concurrent meningiomas, as well as previously undescribed familial *Aip* gene mutations. The clinical spectrum of *AIP*-mutated FIPA ranges from asymptomatic presentations in adult/elderly individuals to large, aggressive early-onset pituitary tumors. In *AIP* mutation-negative FIPA kindreds, variants in the *CDKN1B* gene have been evaluated. FIPA is also categorized alongside other inherited endocrine tumor predisposition syndromes, specifically Carney's syndrome and hyperparathyroidism type 2 (HRPT2), which are associated with inactivating mutations in the *PRKAR1-alpha* and *HRPT2* genes, respectively.

This review summarizes currently available clinical data regarding Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenoma (FIPA) patients, specifically distinguishing between AIP mutation-positive and AIP mutation-negative cohorts.

Heterozygous mutations in the *AIP* gene are identified in approximately 20% of Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenoma (FIPA) families, a figure consistent with the broader reported range of 15–25% for *AIP*-associated FIPA cases.

In 20–40% of families with this syndrome, mutations have been identified in the aryl hydrocarbon receptor interacting protein gene, while the causative gene or genes remain unidentified in the remaining families.

Familial isolated pituitary adenoma (FIPA) is an autosomal-dominant disease with variable penetrance, in which germline heterozygous mutations in the tumor suppressor aryl hydrocarbon receptor interacting protein (AIP) gene explain the condition in 20% of patients/families, while no gene abnormality has been identified to date in the majority of FIPA families.

The 2006 discovery of heterozygous, loss-of-function germline mutations in the gene encoding the aryl hydrocarbon receptor interacting protein (AIP) enabled the identification of such mutations in 20% of FIPA families and 20% of childhood-onset simplex somatotroph adenomas.

Molecular genetic factors unequivocally linked to pituitary tumours are limited to four specific entities: (1) GNAS1 activation in acromegaly; (2) MENIN and p27Kip1 (CDKN1B) mutations associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1; (3) PRKA1RA mutations with loss of 17q22-24 in Carney complex; and (4) aryl hydrocarbon receptor interacting protein gene mutations, which are present in 15% of familial isolated pituitary adenomas and 50% of familial isolated acromegaly.
Understanding the tumorigenic process in AIP-positive and AIP-negative FIPA patients may yield improved diagnostic and treatment options for both familial and sporadic cases.

Ninety-one tumors from 31 NF1 patients were screened for gross changes in the NF1 gene using microsatellite/restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) markers; loss of heterozygosity (LOH) was found in 17 out of 91 (19%) tumors (including two out of seven MPNSTs). Denaturing high performance liquid chromatography (DHPLC) was then used to screen 43 LOH-negative and 10 LOH-positive tumors for NF1 microlesions at both RNA and DNA levels. Thirteen germline and 12 somatic mutations were identified, of which three germline (IVS7-2A>G, 3731delT, 6117delG) and eight somatic (1888delG, 4374-4375delCC, R2129S, 2088delG, 2341del18, IVS27b-5C>T, 4083insT, Q519P) were novel. A mosaic mutation (R2429X) was also identified in a neurofibroma by DHPLC analysis and cloning/sequencing.

Ninety-one tumors from 31 NF1 patients were screened for gross changes in the NF1 gene using microsatellite/restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) markers; loss of heterozygosity (LOH) was found in 17 out of 91 (19%) tumors (including two out of seven MPNSTs). Denaturing high performance liquid chromatography (DHPLC) was then used to screen 43 LOH-negative and 10 LOH-positive tumors for NF1 microlesions at both RNA and DNA levels. Thirteen germline and 12 somatic mutations were identified, of which three germline (IVS7-2A>G, 3731delT, 6117delG) and eight somatic (1888delG, 4374-4375delCC, R2129S, 2088delG, 2341del18, IVS27b-5C>T, 4083insT, Q519P) were novel. A mosaic mutation (R2429X) was also identified in a neurofibroma by DHPLC analysis and cloning/sequencing.

Identifying the specific genetic defect is challenging due to the gene's extreme size and a high incidence of sporadic mutations distributed across the entire gene, which range from single nucleotide substitutes to large deletions.

Molecular characterization of the *NF1* gene, initially confirmed by cloning a 11–13 kb mRNA encoding region exhibiting deletions and point mutations in affected individuals but not controls, reveals a diverse mutational spectrum. 4H syndrome is a rare, newly recognized, and distinct leukodystrophy characterized by the triad of hypomyelination, hypodontia, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. It represents one of five overlapping clinical phenotypes—previously described as distinct entities prior to the identification of their molecular basis—that include: Hypomyelination, hypodontia, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (4H syndrome); Ataxia, delayed dentition, and hypomyelination (ADDH); Tremor-ataxia with central hypomyelination (TACH); Leukodystrophy with oligodontia (LO); and Hypomyelination with cerebellar atrophy and hypoplasia of the corpus callosum (HCAHC).

MRI findings of diffuse cerebral hypomyelination, cerebellar atrophy, and a thin corpus callosum, combined with X-ray evidence of persistent milk teeth and hypoplastic crowns and roots, are indicative of 4H syndrome (hypomyelination, hypodontia, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism).

Families mapped to the same locus as leukodystrophy with oligodontia (LO) and exhibiting clinical and radiological overlap with hypomyelination, hypodontia and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (4H) syndrome were subjected to gene sequencing in nine individuals with 4H and eight with LO.

level_2.text: 4H syndrome is a rare, distinct leukodystrophy defined by the triad of hypomyelination, hypodontia, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, accompanied by slowly progressive encephalopathy and ataxia. It represents one of five overlapping clinical phenotypes—previously considered distinct entities prior to molecular identification—that include Hypomyelination, hypodontia, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (4H); Ataxia, delayed dentition, and hypomyelination (ADDH); Tremor-ataxia with central hypomyelination (TACH); Leukodystrophy with oligodontia (LO); and Hypomyelination with cerebellar atrophy and hypoplasia of the corpus callosum (HCAHC). Diagnostic imaging reveals diffuse cerebral hypomyelination, cerebellar atrophy, and a thin corpus callosum on MRI, while X-rays show persistent milk teeth with hypoplastic crowns and roots. Genetic studies have mapped families with 4H syndrome to the same locus as LO, with gene sequencing performed on nine individuals with 4H and eight with LO to investigate this clinical and radiological overlap.

level_1.text: BRCA1 functions as an E3 ubiquitin ligase that mediates transcriptional repression by ubiquitinating the transcriptional preinitiation complex. This ubiquitin-dependent modification prevents the stable association of TFIIE and TFIIH, thereby blocking the initiation of mRNA synthesis.

The BRCA1 tumor suppressor gene, expressed in all mammalian cells, encodes a protein that functions as an E3 ubiquitin ligase in complex with BARD1. While this enzymatic activity is thought to be required for tumor suppression in normal breast and ovarian cells, it is not essential for mammalian cell viability or homology-directed repair of double-strand DNA breaks. During DNA replication and repair, BRCA1 serves dual roles: as an adaptor for the transient physical recruitment of proteins including NBS1, gammaH2AX, and FANCD2 into specific repair-associated complexes, and as an enzyme exerting E3-ubiquitin ligase activity against a subset of these proteins. The BRCA1 protein interacts with several distinct nuclear complexes, whose constituent proteins represent potential targets for the BRCA1:BARD1 E3-ubiquitin ligase activity.

The sole known enzymatic activity of BRCA1 is E3-ubiquitin ligase function, mediated by its N-terminal RING finger domain. This activity is tightly regulated by the dimeric binding partner BARD1, with which BRCA1 forms a heterodimeric complex in vivo; this complex’s enzymatic activity is conserved across a broad phylogenetic range and is further modulated by cancer mutations and diverse signaling pathways. Structurally, the arrangement of the Ring-domains in the BRCA1/BARD1 complex resembles that of the H2A E3 ligase complex formed by Ring1b and Bmi1, although the latter’s complex formation specifically depends on an N-terminal arm of Ring1b embracing the Bmi1 Ring-domain.

level_2.text: BRCA1, a tumor suppressor expressed in all mammalian cells, functions as an E3 ubiquitin ligase within a heterodimeric complex with BARD1, an activity mediated by its N-terminal RING finger domain and structurally resembling the Ring1b/Bmi1 H2A E3 ligase complex, though the latter specifically depends on an N-terminal arm of Ring1b embracing the Bmi1 Ring-domain. This enzymatic activity, which is conserved across a broad phylogenetic range and modulated by cancer mutations and diverse signaling pathways, mediates transcriptional repression by ubiquitinating the transcriptional preinitiation complex, thereby preventing the stable association of TFIIE and TFIIH and blocking mRNA synthesis initiation. While this activity is thought to be required for tumor suppression in normal breast and ovarian cells, it is not essential for mammalian cell viability or homology-directed repair of double-strand DNA breaks. During DNA replication and repair, BRCA1 serves dual roles: as an adaptor for the transient physical recruitment of proteins including NBS1, gammaH2AX, and FANCD2 into specific repair-associated complexes, and as an enzyme exerting E3-ubiquitin ligase activity against a subset of these proteins

level_1.text: CD56 expression is a highly significant independent prognostic marker for progression-free survival (PFS), with low/negative expression associated with 69% PFS versus 30% in high expression groups (P = 0.024). In patients with localized nonpelvic disease, low/negative CD56 expression yielded 100% PFS compared to 40% in the high expressing group (P = 0.02), and CD56 was identified as an independent prognostic marker conferring an 11-fold increased risk for relapse in patients with localized disease (P = 0.006).

CD56 expression serves as a prognostic biomarker for Ewing sarcoma (ES) patients, enabling the identification of individuals with excellent prognosis versus those predisposed to relapse, thereby facilitating improved treatment stratification and the implementation of personalized therapy.

Flow cytometry identification of CD56 (and CD57) at diagnosis defines a subset of Ewing sarcoma patients with an excellent prognosis. In contrast, a case of severe respiratory difficulty three years post-diagnosis revealed multiple tumors with high-grade sarcoma foci compatible with primitive neuroectodermal tumor/extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma, confirmed by morphology and immunohistochemistry for CD99 and CD56.

In patients with localized nonpelvic disease, low/negative CD56 expression yielded 100% PFS compared to 40% in the high expressing group (P = 0.02), and CD56 was identified as an independent prognostic marker conferring an 11-fold increased risk for relapse in patients with localized disease (P = 0.006). Conversely, a case of severe respiratory difficulty three years post-diagnosis revealed multiple tumors with high-grade sarcoma foci compatible with primitive neuroectodermal tumor/extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma, confirmed by morphology and immunohistochemistry for CD99 and CD56.
